newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Filipino businessmen stage strike over kidnappings.
newsitem.headline: Filipino businessmen stage strike over kidnappings.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday he might seek the aid of former Moslem rebel chief Nur Misuari to stop kidnappings in the southern Philippines after businessmen closed their shops in protest at the crime wave.
Ramos said he had ordered Interior Secretary Robert Barbers to study the possibility of asking Misuari to take "an active hand" in curbing a series of kidnappings in southern Cotabato city.
"This is where (he) can play a very important preventive, maybe, operational role," Ramos told his weekly news conference.

Misuari has joined the Ramos administration as governor of a semi-autonomous Moslem region after signing a peace deal with Manila recently ending a 24-year revolt for Moslem self-rule led by the Moro National Liberationt Front (MNLF), which he heads.

Thirteen kidnap-for-ransom incidents have occurred in Cotabato this month. Six of the victims, including a priest, two children and a Filipino-Chinese businessman are still in captivity, Chinese community officials said.
Members of some of the kidnap gangs are suspected to be former Moslem guerrillas who had turned to banditry, police said.
The Cotabato abductions coincided with an upsurge of kidnapping cases in the capital, Manila.
Scores of shops in Cotabato shut down their businessess on Wednesday in protest against government failure to stop the kidnappers.

The shutdowns were a show of "full indignation over such atrocity that now happen openly and without letup ... causing deep anger among the citizenry who deserve much protection from the government and its so-called authorities," the Filipino-Chinese chambers of commerce of Cotabato and Manila said in a statement.
The statement was signed by Manila chamber president and industrial magnate Lucio Tan and by Cotabato chamber head Oscar Tan Abing.

In the latest incident, gunmen on Tuesday shot dead the wife of local Chinese businessman Apo Chua and wounded the businessman himself, his driver and a civilian in a failed kidnapping attempt in a busy street in Cotabato.
The kidnappers fired on Chua's car when it refused to stop after they had blocked the vehicle.

Kidnap gangs abducted a total of 114 people in the first nine months of this year and collected 36.2 million pesos ($1.35 million) in ransom, according to official statistics. Thirty-seven of the incidents occurred in the Manila area.
Widespread suspicions that the gangs are protected by senior police officers have discouraged families of victims from cooperating with the authorities.
